scenes.title: Intermanual Conflict at the Neurology Exam Table: Right Hand Buttoning a Crisp Shirt While the Rogue Left Hand Unbuttons It
scenes.era: 1981 / 1992, Philadelphia & New York behavioral neurology clinic

layout.description: Sunlit clinical neurology examination room with an oak exam desk holding everyday affordance test objects (a porcelain mug, wooden hairbrush, and folded towel) as a patient sits upright wearing a crisp pale-blue button-down cardigan shirt.

positions.where: using their right hand to carefully fasten the middle shirt buttons while their own left hand smoothly reaches up two buttons lower to unfasten them — looking down in startled exasperation

positions.who: Neurologist mannequin (Gary Goldberg / Todd Feinberg in white coat with clipboard)
positions.where: observing the smooth opposite-hand tug-of-war before handing a soft white grip cylinder to occupy the rogue hand

props.name: large-buttoned pale-blue clinical test shirt
props.period_detail: shows right hand buttoning upward while left hand unbuttons right behind it
props.physical_behavior: the single most iconic bedside sign of Callosal intermanual conflict

props.name: desktop affordance tray (porcelain mug, wooden comb, doorknob block)
props.period_detail: triggers compulsive one-handed reaching in the Frontal SMA variant

props.name: soft white foam 'Occupy-the-Hand' rehabilitation cylinder
props.period_detail: calms compulsive environmental grasping when held in the rogue palm

actions.verb_sequence: fastens two buttons smoothly with the right hand -> left hand glides in uninvited and unbuttons them -> Patient uses right hand to gently hold their own left wrist while looking at the neurologist
places the soft foam cylinder into the rogue hand -> compulsive reaching quiets immediately

reactions.reaction: shakes head in clear-minded disbelief ('It is my hand, Doctor, it just won't listen!')
maps Frontal SMA vs Callosal fibers on the bedside chart

scenes.wardrobe: 1980s/1990s clinical neurology coat with tie; pale-blue large-button Oxford shirt and chinos.
scenes.recognition_hook: His right hand buttons his shirt to get dressed — and two seconds later his own left hand smoothly unbuttons every single button.

key_visual.description: a neurology clinic scene where a seated patient's right hand buttons a pale-blue shirt while their own left hand simultaneously unbuttons it across from a neurologist with an object test tray

scenes.title: Goldberg 1981 Frontal Variant: The Doorframe Grasp That Won't Let Go

layout.description: Bright sunlit hospital corridor doorway with a wooden handrail.

positions.where: walking past a doorframe as one hand shoots out automatically to latch onto the wooden rail, requiring the intact hand to gently peel the fingers loose

props.name: wooden doorway handle & soft rolled towel
props.period_detail: visualizes unbraked SMA environmental affordance grasping and the towel-holding fix

actions.verb_sequence: latches smoothly onto doorframe -> intact hand peels fingers off and places rolled towel in palm -> patient walks smoothly onward

reactions.reaction: nods encouragingly as towel-holding restores smooth walking

scenes.recognition_hook: Without the medial-frontal veto brake, every doorknob in sight commands the hand to grab — unless you give the palm something safe to hold.

scenes.title: Feinberg 1992: One Name, Three Separate Brain Circuits

layout.description: Bright teaching table displaying three clean matte-white 3D anatomical brain models highlighting Medial Frontal (SMA), Corpus Callosum, and Posterior Parietal zones.

positions.where: pointing across the three anatomical zones to explain Grasp vs Intermanual Conflict vs Levitation

props.name: trio of color-coded matte-white brain models
props.period_detail: clarifies why Frontal, Callosal, and Parietal lesions look completely different at the bedside

actions.verb_sequence: traces SMA grasp release vs Callosal hand-fighting vs Parietal sensory levitation

reactions.reaction: take notes resolving decades of clinical confusion

scenes.recognition_hook: Not one mysterious curse — three precise wiring breaks separating grasp brakes, hemisphere teamwork, and limb feedback.

scenes.title: Everyday Affordance Hygiene: Out of Sight Saves Your Veto Brake

layout.description: Sunlit tidy desk where placing a phone and snack bowl inside a closed wooden drawer stops unconscious hand reaches.

positions.where: tucking phone into drawer so premotor affordance triggers stop firing every minute

props.name: closed desk drawer vs open tabletop phone

actions.verb_sequence: places phone out of sight -> types deeply with zero unconscious reaches

scenes.recognition_hook: Even healthy brains secretly prep a reach every time eyes hit a phone or cookie — put distractions out of sight so your frontal brake can rest.
